title: Is it death and its reversals that make you grieve?
intro: Al-Sukkari transmits al-Asma'i's account that Abu Dhu'ayb lost five sons to plague in a single year. Umayma first sees the bereavement in the colour of his face and his inability to lie still. His answer ranges out from the bed to wild asses surprised at water, a bull pursued by hounds and two equally matched horsemen. The words “every flank has its place to fall” return when the bull lies in the dust. Osama al-Nahari recites a sixty-nine-line transmission, longer than the main text of al-Sukkari's commentary.

translation: Is it death and its reversals that make you grieve?
Time will make no amends to anyone who grieves.
1.sharh: He addresses himself as someone who has lodged a complaint. Time is imagined as a person capable of granting redress, then the possibility is withdrawn.

translation: Umayma said, “Why is your body so pale
since you took that labour on yourself, with wealth enough to help?
2.sharh: Umayma sees a man worn down by work he now does for himself. His wealth could pay someone to take it off his hands. She has yet to hear what the loss of his sons means to him.

translation: And why can your side find no bed to fit it
without that bed turning rough beneath you?”
3.sharh: The bed seems to change its texture when he lies down. What she sees as physical restlessness is the grief he has yet to name.

translation: I answered her, “What ails my body is this.
My sons have passed from the land and taken their leave.
4.sharh: Only now does he name the sons. The language of leaving one's country makes death sound almost like a family departure, except that nobody is coming back.

translation: My sons are gone. They left me a catch in my throat
when others have fallen asleep, and tears that will not stop.
5.sharh: The sons leave their father an inheritance he feels in his throat and eyes. The old commentary takes the sleepers to be the people around him. He is awake after the house has fallen quiet.

translation: They outpaced my wish and sped away with theirs.
They were taken off. Every flank has its place to fall.
6.sharh: At first the sons seem almost to choose a faster course than their father. The sudden passive verb gives them back to the death that carried them away.

translation: I lingered after them in a life of toil.
I think I too shall be made to follow.
7.sharh: The survivor's verb means remaining after others are gone. He imagines a summons that will put the father behind the children on the same road.

translation: How hard I tried to fend death away from them.
Once it comes towards you, it cannot be turned back.
8.sharh: His care takes the form of a physical attempt to push something back. The second half makes its advance irreversible.

translation: Once death has sunk its claws in,
you find every amulet powerless.
9.sharh: The claws that catch and the amulet that hangs near the skin come together in one image. What was carried for protection cannot loosen death's grip.

translation: Since their loss my eyes are as if their pupils
had been pierced with thorns, blinded and streaming.
10.sharh: The tears are as physical as injury to an eye. Umayma can see them, but only the father can feel the imagined thorns.

translation: To misfortunes I have become a flint
on the rock of al-Musharraq, struck every day.
11.sharh: The flint is hard, yet it has no escape from repeated blows. The place name evokes a much-frequented rock at Mina in the old explanation.

translation: Destruction waits and cannot be escaped. Wait and see
whether your fall will come at home or in another land.
12.sharh: Death is settled like a resident, while its future victim may travel. What remains open is the geography of the fall.

translation: I know full well that weeping is folly.
Yet whoever suffers loss will be given over to tears.
13.sharh: The second half acknowledges what the first half's judgement leaves out. The bereaved person can understand the futility of weeping and still be claimed by it.

translation: Your own day will surely come,
when you lie covered, wept over, hearing nothing.
14.sharh: The mourner is made to look ahead to the covered face on the other side of grief. The loss of hearing completes the reversal.

translation: I stand firm before those who gloat, to show them
that I do not buckle under time's blows.
15.sharh: Endurance has an audience. Its public purpose explains how the same man can look unshaken and lie awake in tears.

translation: The self is full of wants if you encourage them.
Turn it back to little and it will be content.
16.sharh: Desire learns from practice. The maxim about making do with little is also a father's attempt to teach himself how to go on.

translation: How many companies, close-knit and all of one mind,
have spent a night at ease, then scattered.
17.sharh: A group at ease together in the evening can wake into dispersal. The “crack” at the end runs through what affection seemed to have made whole.

translation: If time and its reversals have bereaved me of them,
I have often been bereaved of those I love.
18.sharh: The emphatic last word describes a man struck by loss again and again. Remembering former losses deepens the present one.

translation: Against the blows of time no one endures,
even the unassailable on a towering peak.
19.sharh: The line leaves the creature unnamed. Commentators envisage an ibex on an inaccessible height, a first test of how much protection a place can give.

translation: Against the blows of time there will not last
the dark-backed wild ass and his four dry jennies.
20.sharh: The refrain now introduces a whole small society. Its four females and dark-backed male are individuated before the reader sees them threatened.

translation: His throat rings out as though he were always
a slave of Abu Rabi'a's house crying out at a beast.
21.sharh: The comparison is heard before it is seen. One old interpretation imagines a herdsman raising the alarm when a predator falls on his flock.

translation: He cropped the young grass. A long-backed jenny yielded to him,
straight as a spear shaft. Rich pastures made him frisk.
22.sharh: New grass, a willing mate and vigorous play make up a season of plenty. The straight shaft is a comparison for the jenny's long body.

translation: In the hollows of flats watered by a downpour,
the sky split open and poured for a spell without ceasing.
23.sharh: The ground is shaped to hold water. The rain's unbroken fall accounts for the richness in which the animals have been living.

translation: For a while the jennies jostled in a meadow.
Sometimes he wrestled in earnest, sometimes in play.
24.sharh: There is time to tell play from earnest play-fighting. Later in the same story that freedom of movement will disappear.

translation: Then the waters of his upland hollows ebbed,
and at what a time in the long season they ran out.
25.sharh: The water disappears precisely when the animals most need it. The exclamation prepares the decision to seek a new watering place.

translation: He thought of taking them to water. Ill fortune crossed
his purpose, and his appointed end came on his trail.
26.sharh: A sensible provision for the herd becomes the beginning of its end. Fate already tracks the stallion before the human hunter has entered the scene.

translation: He drove them in turns down from the high ground, whose water
was plentiful. A broad track came across his course.
27.sharh: The stallion takes command of the descent. The wide track crossing his course gives the animals a visible route towards the encounter.

translation: At the valley bend between Yunabi'
and the slopes of Dhu al-Arja', they looked like gathered spoil.
28.sharh: Herding begins to resemble the driving off of captured camels. The two landmarks fix this sudden likeness to a particular valley.

translation: They were like a bundle of gaming arrows, and he
a player casting the lots and calling them out.
29.sharh: The animals cluster and separate like lots in a draw. Their driver both handles the moving pieces and supplies the gambler's cry.

translation: He was like a whetstone turning over and over
in the palm, only he was the thicker of the two.
30.sharh: The stone gives a shape to the stallion's solidity and turning motion. The last qualification insists on the greater bulk of the living animal.

translation: They came to water. Capella kept watch like a lookout
over men drawing lots, above the row of stars, craning no higher.
31.sharh: In the late sky Capella sits just above the star group as an observer sits over the men drawing lots. The gambling image has moved from earth to sky.

translation: They stepped into the margins of cool fresh water,
its bed pebbled, its depth swallowing their shanks.
32.sharh: The pebbles suggest clarity and the vanishing legs show the depth. The pool briefly offers everything the journey promised.

translation: They drank, then heard a sound beyond
a rise that screened it, a suspicious knocking.
33.sharh: The cause of the noise is hidden by a rise. The reader shares the animals' uncertainty for a moment before the man is disclosed.

translation: A tautly belted hunter let slip a telltale sound.
In his hand were a deep-voiced bow and short, broad arrowheads.
34.sharh: The noise betrays a man who had kept himself out of sight. Even the bow has a voice, deep in contrast with the tiny sound the herd first noticed.

translation: They shied from him and bolted. The two leaders jostled,
the long-necked jenny and the deep-flanked stallion.
35.sharh: Jenny and stallion both take the front as the herd breaks. Their collision makes the sudden change from orderly progress to panic visible.

translation: He shot at a tall jenny that had gone a season barren.
The arrow went through and fell, its feathers clotted together.
36.sharh: The thing that falls at the end is the shaft. Its stuck feathers tell what has happened to the jenny without directly describing her wound.

translation: The stallion's flanks showed as he swerved hastily away.
The man was already rummaging back in his quiver.
37.sharh: The point of view switches from the turning flank to the searching hand. Neither animal nor hunter is still for an instant.

translation: He let fly a far-reaching shaft from Sa'da.
It lodged in the stallion’s flank, and the ribs closed round it.
38.sharh: The stallion who led the whole journey is reached at last. Motion ends in the image of ribs enclosing the shaft that entered his side.

translation: He dealt them out their deaths. One fled
on its last breath, another crouched pressed to the ground.
39.sharh: Giving each its portion recalls the earlier casting of lots. What appears to be a choice between flight and collapse is now only a difference in how life ends.

translation: They stumbled on the sharp edges as though
their forelegs had been clothed in Banu Yazid's striped mantles.
40.sharh: Streams of blood leave a pattern like dyed stripes on woven cloth. Clothing the forelegs is an exact visual comparison with a bitterly incongruous finery.

translation: Against the blows of time there will not last
a full-grown bull driven wild with fear by hounds.
41.sharh: The refrain moves to another animal in its prime. The hounds are already present in the words that introduce him, long before the actual encounter.

translation: The hunting dogs have laid his heart bare to fear.
Whenever he sees the true dawn he takes fright.
42.sharh: Daybreak is enough by itself to alarm him. Past encounters have made him read the coming of light as the approach of hunters.

translation: He shelters under the arta shrubs whenever rain numbs him
and a cold driving wind finds him at evening.
43.sharh: The shrub provides a real refuge for the night. Its protection answers the weather alone and has a definite end at morning.

translation: His eyes probe what is hidden. Half-lowered, his gaze
looks for confirmation of everything he hears.
44.sharh: Sight and hearing continually check one another. Even a lowered gaze is part of a watchfulness that never lets him rest.

translation: He turns his back to the morning sun. There appear
the foremost hounds, close by, being held in check.
45.sharh: He has only just come out to dry himself in the sun. Holding back the fastest hounds, in al-Asma'i's reading, gives the pack time to gather.

translation: He started in fright. All his openings were closed
by grey, seasoned hounds, two whole-eared and one cropped.
46.sharh: The pack closes the gaps around him. The detail of the cropped ear distinguishes one animal among three as clearly as the herd's markings did before.

translation: They snap at him. He drives them back and holds his ground,
thick-shanked, streaked with colour on both flanks.
47.sharh: A rapid exchange of bites and rebuffs is interrupted by a close view of the bull's legs and markings. His power and vulnerability are in the same body.

translation: He turned on them with two keen points, as though
the stirred spatter on them were red dragon's-blood resin.
48.sharh: The two points are the bull's horns. A red dye supplies the colour of the liquid his movement has stirred over them.

translation: They were like two spits untouched as yet by roasting smoke,
hurried into meat that drinkers were pulling off.
49.sharh: The horns appear like a pair of spits put to use and withdrawn before the roast can give off its smell. The impatient drinkers supply the speed of the image.

translation: They brought him down in the dust, his flank
caked with earth. Every flank has its place to fall.
50.sharh: The father's words about his sons return exactly as the bull's side touches earth. A general statement of mortality has become a place one can see.

translation: When they drew back, he had felled a group of them,
and the surviving straggler stood cowering.
51.sharh: The account turns to the damage the fallen animal has done. A survivor of the pack stands in the posture of helplessness once associated with the prey.

translation: Then the hounds' master appeared to him, in his hand
bright thin heads on shafts with close-trimmed feathers.
52.sharh: The bull could answer the dogs with his horns. The bright heads and trimmed feathers announce a man who can reach him from farther away.

translation: He shot to save the fleeing hounds. In their defence flew
an arrow that pierced both stripes on the bull’s flanks.
53.sharh: The dogs give their master a reason to shoot. The two stripes that marked the bull's living body now mark the path of the shaft through it. The printed masculine pronoun turns attention straight back to the bull.

translation: He toppled like a stiffening camel stallion
on low open ground, save that the camel towers higher.
54.sharh: The open ground gives an uninterrupted view of the fall. An old gloss takes the final comparison to qualify the scale, since the camel is the larger beast.

translation: Against the blows of time there will not last
a helmeted man wearing rings of iron against his skin.
55.sharh: This time the creature equipped to resist is a human being. Armour can bring him safely into the encounter which will prove its limits.

translation: The mail grew hot on him until his face
was darkened by its heat on the day of battle.
56.sharh: Protection has a physical cost before anyone strikes a blow. Darkening of the face makes the battle heat visible.

translation: A deep-eyed mare carries him, her gallop wrenching
the saddle rings apart, though her running is loose and flowing.
57.sharh: The strain shows in the fittings of the saddle. The mare herself still moves with an easy stride, which makes the force of the movement more striking.

translation: He reserved the morning milk for her, marbling her flesh
with fat so deep a finger sinks into it.
58.sharh: The rider's care has softened the mare's flesh until a finger sinks into it. Al-Asma'i objected that a horse this fat would soon tire at a gallop.

translation: Her thigh sinews stand in relief above a dark-red udder,
like an earring, shrunk, with no milk for a foal.
59.sharh: The earring gives both the size and the suspended shape of the udder. The absence of a suckling foal helps explain the mare's condition.

translation: Pressed hard, she withholds her flow,
save for the hot sweat that wells out in drops.
60.sharh: “Flow” can describe a mare giving her full speed or an udder giving milk, and the commentators divide. What can actually be seen breaking out is sweat.

translation: As he grappled with armoured men and wheeled away,
one day a bold, unflinching opponent was allotted to him.
61.sharh: A lifetime of familiar encounters meets a single answering opponent. The passive verb makes their meeting sound appointed, like the place of falling earlier in the poem.

translation: His mount runs with light-boned joints, like
a hill goat sure in its stride, free of any limp.
62.sharh: The newcomer too has a sound, agile mount. By giving the second horse its own comparison the poet makes the two riders equals before they meet.

translation: They called to one another and their horses stood face to face.
Each was a battle champion schooled in its deceits.
63.sharh: The paired verbs stop the movement of both horses. Experience belongs equally to both men, down to the wariness learnt from earlier tricks.

translation: Each guarded his glory against the other, each confident
in his own proven worth on this grim day.
64.sharh: Their courage has already been tested elsewhere. The repeated “each” prevents the reader from picking a favourite or predicting a victor.

translation: Over them lay two woven coats of mail, finished
by David or by Tubba', master of long coats of mail.
65.sharh: David was proverbial for making mail, and fine armour was attributed to the kings of Himyar. The names imagine craftsmanship equal to everything these men possess.

translation: Each held a Yazani spear in his hand,
with a polished head bright as a lamp.
66.sharh: The place-name distinguishes the quality of the spear. The lamp comparison picks out the flash from its smooth head as the two men face one another.

translation: Each wore slung about him a blade with a sheen,
sharp enough to cut whatever it touched.
67.sharh: Yet another shared possession makes the contest more perfectly matched. Neither man can gain the advantage the careful description of his blade might lead us to expect.

translation: Each snatched the other's life with piercing wounds,
like openings cut in new cloth that no one patches.
68.sharh: A tailor cuts openings for the neck and cuffs of a new garment and leaves them open. So too the wounds will never close. Each of the evenly matched riders takes the other’s life.

translation: Each had lived the life of a man of honour
and gathered glory, if anything at all could avail.”
69.sharh: They really did gain honour. The condition attached to its value returns to Umayma's early confidence that wealth might help, and the father's reply is complete.

1.1.2.head: المَنون
1.1.2.meaning: Death, or time as the power that cuts a life short.

1.1.3.head: الرَّيب
1.1.3.meaning: Its unpredictable reversals, especially the strokes that take people away.

1.2.3.head: أَعتَبَ
1.2.3.meaning: Grant someone redress or give satisfaction for a grievance.

2.2.2.head: اِبتَذَلَ
2.2.2.meaning: To put oneself to hard work. The passive reading means “you were worn down by drudgery”.

3.2.2.meaning: Become rough and keep a sleeper turning, as grit would beneath the body.

4.2.1.meaning: Perish. The sons themselves are the subject of the verb.

4.2.5.head: وَدَّعَ
4.2.5.meaning: Take leave. Al-Sukkari and the reciter join the farewell with “and”. The Cairo diwan and Mufaddaliyyat read fa-, “and so”.

5.1.4.head: غُصَّة
5.1.4.meaning: A catch in the throat, the bodily sensation left by grief.

5.2.3.head: عَبرَة
5.2.3.meaning: A tear drawn by grief. The following verb says it never lets up.

6.1.3.head: أَعنَقَ
6.1.3.meaning: Travel at a swift, free stride, originally of camels.

6.2.1.head: تُخُرِّمَ
6.2.1.meaning: To be taken off by death, as if torn from one's company.

7.1.1.head: غَبَرَ
7.1.1.meaning: Remain behind after others have gone.

7.2.4.head: مُستَتبَع
7.2.4.meaning: One summoned to follow those who have gone before.

8.1.2.head: حَرِصَ
8.1.2.meaning: To strive eagerly for something. The two classical vowel forms mean the same thing. Here the father is doing all he can to keep his sons alive.

9.1.3.head: أَنشَبَ
9.1.3.meaning: Drive in and fasten, like claws gripping prey.

9.2.3.head: تَميمَة
9.2.3.meaning: An amulet worn in the hope of warding off harm.

10.1.4.head: حَدَقَة
10.1.4.meaning: The dark central part of the eye.

10.2.1.meaning: Were put out or made sightless by piercing.

11.1.4.head: مَروَة
11.1.4.meaning: A hard pale flint exposed here to repeated blows.

11.2.2.head: المُشَرَّق
11.2.2.meaning: A site at Mina in the old commentary. Another reading names al-Mushaqqar.

13.2.3.head: بُكاء
13.2.3.meaning: Weeping. Arabic has both buka' and the shorter buka. Both forms occur in this line.

14.2.3.head: مُقَنَّع
14.2.3.meaning: With the face covered, as the dead are laid out.

15.2.5.head: تَضَعضَعَ
15.2.5.meaning: Give way or buckle, as something once firmly built might do.

17.2.4.head: تَصَدَّعَ
17.2.4.meaning: Break apart. A crack running through one thing supplies the image of dispersal.

18.2.4.head: مُفَجَّع
18.2.4.meaning: Someone who has been bereaved repeatedly.

19.1.5.head: حَدَثان
19.1.5.meaning: The successive blows of time. The expression returns as each new instance begins.

19.2.5.head: مُمَنَّع
19.2.5.meaning: Strongly protected or inaccessible on its height.

20.2.1-2.head: جَونُ السَّراة
20.2.1-2.meaning: Dark along the ridge of the back. The animal is a wild jackass.

20.2.4.head: جَدود
20.2.4.meaning: Jennies with little or no milk, the four females with the stallion.

21.1.2.head: شارِب
21.1.2.meaning: The passages in the throat from which the bray rings out.

21.2.5.head: مُسبَع
21.2.5.meaning: One crying out because a predator is among the flock. Another gloss is someone left to grow wild among beasts.

22.1.2.head: الجَميم
22.1.2.meaning: Fresh shoots of grass, thick and still low.

22.1.4.head: سَمحَج
22.1.4.meaning: A long-backed jenny, her straight body likened to a spear shaft.

22.2.4.head: الأَمرُع
22.2.4.meaning: Rich grazing grounds that have put life into the stallion.

23.2.2.head: أَثجَمَ
23.2.2.meaning: Keep pouring down, or discharge rain rapidly. The next words stress its duration.

24.1.3.head: اِعتَلَجَ
24.1.3.meaning: Jostle and grapple with one another in the vigour of play.

24.2.5.head: شَمَعَ
24.2.5.meaning: Play or romp, in alternation with earnest wrestling.

25.1.5.head: رَزن
25.1.5.meaning: Raised ground with hollows that catch the rain.

25.2.3.head: مِلاوَة
25.2.3.meaning: A stretch of time, here the season in which the water gives out.

26.2.3.head: حَين
26.2.3.meaning: His death or appointed end, imagined as a tracker on his trail.

27.1.1.head: اِفتَنَّ
27.1.1.meaning: Drive the herd on in varying ways, changing the manner of urging it.

27.2.1.head: بَثر
27.2.1.meaning: Abundant, describing the water of the place.

27.2.4.head: مَهيَع
27.2.4.meaning: A broad, open track crossing their route.

28.1.2.head: جِزع
28.1.2.meaning: The bend of a valley or watercourse.

28.2.4.head: نَهب
28.2.4.meaning: Spoil taken in a raid, pictured here as a compact drove of captured camels.

29.1.2.head: رِبابَة
29.1.2.meaning: A set of gaming arrows, or the cloth in which they were gathered.

29.2.1.head: يَسَر
29.2.1.meaning: A player who draws the gaming arrows and apportions the lots.

30.1.3.head: مِدوَس
30.1.3.meaning: A polisher's whetstone turned in the palm.

30.2.6.head: أَضلَع
30.2.6.meaning: Thicker and more substantial in build than the whetstone.

31.1.2.head: العَيّوق
31.1.2.meaning: Capella, a bright star that looks down on the neighbouring group like a lookout.

31.1.4.head: رابِئ
31.1.4.meaning: A lookout seated above the men who draw the lots.

31.2.3.head: النَّظم
31.2.3.meaning: A string of stars identified with Orion. The alternative “the Star” designates the Pleiades.

32.1.3.head: حَجرَة
32.1.3.meaning: Edges or margins, where the herd first enters the pool.

32.2.5.head: كُراع
32.2.5.meaning: The lower legs or shanks, submerged as a measure of the pool's depth.

33.2.1-2.head: شَرَفُ الحِجاب
33.2.1-2.meaning: The high part of the hunter's screen that hides him from the herd.

34.1.1.head: نَميمَة
34.1.1.meaning: A telltale sound, taken by commentators to be that of the bowstring.

34.2.3.head: جَشء
34.2.3.meaning: A light stave, here the wood of a deep-sounding bow.

35.2.1.head: سَطعاء
35.2.1.meaning: Long-necked, describing the jenny at the front.

35.2.4.head: جُرشُع
35.2.4.meaning: Deep-bodied and broad in the flank, said of the stallion.

36.1.3-4.head: نَجود
36.1.3-4.meaning: A tall jenny. The recording has fi, “into”. The Egyptian text has min, “through and out of”.

36.1.5.head: عائِط
36.1.5.meaning: A female that has gone a season without conceiving.

36.2.4.head: مُتَصَمِّع
36.2.4.meaning: Clumped together, of arrow feathers stuck with blood.

37.1.3.head: قُرب
37.1.3.meaning: The flanks exposed by the stallion's swerve.

37.2.2.head: عَيَّثَ
37.2.2.meaning: Rummage in the quiver, feeling for another arrow.

38.1.3.head: صاعِدِيّ
38.1.3.meaning: An epithet for a shaft, derived by Ibn al-Anbari from Sa'da in Yemen. Al-Asma'i left the derivation open.

38.1.4.head: مِطحَر
38.1.4.meaning: A shaft that travels a long distance.

39.1.1.head: أَبَدَّ
39.1.1.meaning: Give each a separate share, here a share in death.

39.2.1.head: ذَماء
39.2.1.meaning: The remnant of life in a mortally wounded animal.

40.1.4.head: ظُبَة
40.1.4.meaning: The points and cutting edges of the arrowheads.

40.2.2.head: بُرد
40.2.2.meaning: Striped woven mantles, evoked by streaks on the animals' legs.

41.2.1.head: شَبَب
41.2.1.meaning: A mature wild bull, or in one gloss an old bull.

42.2.3-4.head: الصُّبحُ المُصَدَّق
42.2.3-4.meaning: True daybreak, when the hunter is accustomed to come out.

43.1.2.head: الأَرطى
43.1.2.meaning: A desert shrub growing in sand, thick enough to shelter wild cattle.

43.2.3-4.head: بَليلٌ زَعزَع
43.2.3-4.meaning: A wet, cold wind that shakes whatever it passes.

44.1.3.head: غَيب
44.1.3.meaning: Hidden places whose far side the bull cannot see.

45.1.2-3.head: شَرَّقَ مَتنَهُ
45.1.2-3.meaning: Turn one's back towards the sun to dry it after the night.

45.2.4.head: وُزِعَ
45.2.4.meaning: Held back until the rest of the pack catches up, according to al-Asma'i. Another gloss is “urged on”.

46.2.3.head: وافٍ
46.2.3.meaning: Two dogs with ears intact beside one with a cropped ear.

47.2.1-2.meaning: Thick-shanked, substantial in the lower limbs.

47.2.4.head: مُوَلَّع
47.2.4.meaning: Streaked with contrasting colours along the flank.

48.1.3.head: مُذَلَّق
48.1.3.meaning: With two smooth keen points, the bull's horns.

48.2.5.head: أَيدَع
48.2.5.meaning: A red dye, identified in one gloss with dragon's-blood resin.

49.1.4.head: أَقتَرَ
49.1.4.meaning: Acquire the smoke or smell of roasting meat. Its absence suggests new spits or a hurried meal.

49.2.4.head: شَرب
49.2.4.meaning: A company of drinkers among whom the roast meat is shared.

51.1.4.head: أَقصَدَ
51.1.4.meaning: Strike home and kill, here what the bull has done to several hounds.

52.2.4.head: مُقَزَّع
52.2.4.meaning: Trimmed or clipped, describing the fletching of the shafts.

53.1.3.head: فَرّ
53.1.3.meaning: The fleeing remnant of the pack.

53.2.4.head: المِنزَع
53.2.4.meaning: A shooting shaft, the subject of the verb “pierced”.

54.1.4-5.head: فَنيقٌ تارِز
54.1.4-5.meaning: A camel stallion gone stiff in death.

54.2.1.head: خَبت
54.2.1.meaning: A low expanse of level ground.

55.2.1.head: مُستَشعِر
55.2.1.meaning: Wearing something against the body, here a coat of linked iron rings.

56.2.5.head: أَسفَع
56.2.5.meaning: Darkened or scorched by the heat against the face.

57.2.2.head: الرِّحالَة
57.2.2.meaning: A leather saddle, including the fastening strained by the mare's pace.

58.1.2.head: الصَّبوح
58.1.2.meaning: The morning draught of milk set aside for the mare.

58.2.1.head: النَّيّ
58.2.1.meaning: Fat that has worked its way through the flesh.

59.1.2.head: نَسا
59.1.2.meaning: The long sinews down the backs of the thighs, showing in relief.

59.2.3.head: غُبر
59.2.3.meaning: The last milk in an udder. The mare's udder has none for a foal.

60.2.2.head: الحَميم
60.2.2.meaning: Hot perspiration breaking out in beads under exertion.

61.2.5.head: سَلفَع
61.2.5.meaning: Bold and formidable, describing the rider who challenges him.

62.1.3-4.head: نَهِشُ المُشاش
62.1.3-4.meaning: Lean at the ends of the bones, a mark of an active, wiry horse.

62.2.1.head: صَدَع
62.2.1.meaning: A medium-sized ibex or antelope, providing a comparison for sound movement.

63.2.4.head: مُخَدَّع
63.2.4.meaning: Seasoned by having been deceived often enough to know the tricks. A reading with dh means repeatedly wounded.

64.2.1.head: بَلاء
64.2.1.meaning: The mettle he has already proved in battle.

65.1.2.head: مَسرودَة
65.1.2.meaning: Two coats of mail made by linking rings.

65.2.5.head: تُبَّع
65.2.5.meaning: A royal title of Himyar, to whose kings a class of armour was ascribed.

66.1.4.head: يَزَنِيَّة
66.1.4.meaning: A spear named for Dhu Yazan of Yemen.

67.2.4.head: الضَّريبَة
67.2.4.meaning: Whatever the blade strikes. Another reading specifies hard things such as bone and iron.

68.2.2.head: العُبُط
68.2.2.meaning: Openings cut on purpose into new cloth, such as neck and sleeve openings, which nobody patches over.

69.2.1-2.head: جَنى العَلاء
69.2.1-2.meaning: Reap glory as one might gather fruit. The condition that follows asks how much it can do against death.

53.1.5.meaning: For the sake of the pack. All three printed witnesses have “for him”, directing the arrow towards the bull.

12.1.4-5.head: تَلَفٌ مُقيم
12.1.4-5.meaning: “An abiding destruction.” Death stays with a person wherever the final meeting takes place. The Egyptian apparatus also gives “one that will befall you”.

16.1.4.head: رَغَّبَ
16.1.4.meaning: To encourage an appetite. The same root first names the soul’s desire, then the act of feeding it.

50.2.1.head: مُتَتَرِّب
50.2.1.meaning: Coated with dust. It clings to the flank on which the bull falls.

2.1.2.head: أُمَيمَة
2.1.2.meaning: Umayma, the woman who notices his pallor and sleeplessness. The father tells of his sons in answer to her.

21.2.2-4.head: آلُ أَبي رَبيعَة
21.2.2-4.meaning: The household of Abu Rabi'a. One gloss identifies him with Shayban, another with Makhzum. The comparison evokes one of a wealthy household’s herdsmen raising the alarm.

28.1.4.head: يُنابِع
28.1.4.meaning: Yunabi', a valley in Hudhayl country. Nubayi' is another form of its name. The herd passes its bend on the way to water.

28.2.1-3.head: أُولاتُ ذي العَرجاء
28.2.1-3.meaning: The stretches of ground around Dhu al-Arja', a hill, according to Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Sukkari writes the same plural without its silent waw.

40.2.3-4.head: بَنو يَزيد
40.2.3-4.meaning: Banu Yazid, associated here with mantles striped in red. Another transmission names Banu Tazid of Quda'a.

65.2.1.head: داوود
65.2.1.meaning: David, famed in Arabic tradition for making coats of mail. The riders wear armour worthy of his workmanship.
